article_title: Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs (English Language Learners)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs — WWC Intervention Report. http://crede.berkeley.edu/research/crede/research/llaa/1.5pubs.html
title: Alternating literature log writing and teacher-facilitated discussion around the same story
description: In the short-term implementation, the two components were "used on alternating days with the same story". Learners first wrote log entries about personal experiences relevant to a character, descriptions of story events, and evaluations of a theme, writing independently and then joining a teacher-led discussion comparing their experiences to the character's. Instructional Conversation lessons then involved teacher-facilitated small-group discussions of story content, approximately 45 minutes per week, giving teachers an opportunity to assess comprehension and broaden understanding of themes.
requirements: Teachers act as discussion facilitators rather than lecturers
Log prompts tied to segments of the same story being discussed
constraints: In the reviewed short-term study the comparison group received less teacher-led instructional time, which confounded the intervention's effects
target_learners: Elementary English language learners
target_learning_goals: Story comprehension
Thematic understanding
English language development
examples: Learners spent at least 45 minutes creating an illustration and caption summarizing their interpretation of the story "Louella's Song" in both intervention and comparison conditions.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs — WWC Intervention Report. http://crede.berkeley.edu/research/crede/research/llaa/1.5pubs.html

article_title: NEW INSIGHTS into Children’s Temperament (INSIGHTS) – Family Engagement
citation: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament. (2010). Program description and evidence summary. https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/insights-into-childrens-temperament/
title: Align educator professional development, classroom sessions, and parent education around a shared temperament framework
description: INSIGHTS works by giving the adults around the child a common framework: educators and parents each receive six self-paced lessons followed by remote facilitated sessions that help them "recognize their children's temperaments/personalities and learn strategies to reduce behavior problems and enhance social skills," while classroom sessions teach children the same temperament ideas. The article presents this three-component alignment as the program's design for improving self-regulation, classroom engagement, and teacher-student relationships.
requirements: Educators and parents complete six one-hour asynchronized and six one-hour synchronized lessons
target_learners: early elementary students and the teachers and families who support them
target_learning_goals: reducing behavior problems
enhancing social skills
improving teacher-student relationships
examples: The trial delivered the program simultaneously to students, teachers, and parents over ten weekly sessions.
key_sources: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament. (2010). Program description and evidence summary. https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/insights-into-childrens-temperament/

article_title: Leveled Literacy Intervention (LLI)
citation: Leveled Literacy Intervention (LLI) evidence summary. (2010). Evidence review of two qualifying studies. https://www.heinemann.com
title: Alternating independent-level and instructional-level texts across tutoring lessons
description: Within LLI, lessons alternate between "independent level" texts and more challenging "instructional level" texts. The instructional-level texts may also be taken back to students' classrooms or homes, extending the tutoring texts into classroom and home reading.
requirements: A supply of leveled texts at both independent and instructional levels for each student
constraints: Applied within a small-group tutoring model for early-grade struggling readers
target_learners: struggling readers in grades K-2
target_learning_goals: reading fluency and comprehension at increasing text difficulty
examples: LLI lessons alternate the two text levels across the 16-18 week tutoring period
key_sources: Leveled Literacy Intervention (LLI) evidence summary. (2010). Evidence review of two qualifying studies. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/fountas-pinnell-leveled-literacy-intervention-lli/

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI)
citation: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org
title: Align Tier 2 supplemental reading instruction with Tier 1 core instruction through teacher professional development and materials
description: The program's central design principle is alignment: it provides "teachers with professional development and materials to improve the alignment of Tier 2 with Tier 1 core instruction." Core reading teachers also receive professional days on the same strategies, so both tiers teach the same content with shared routines.
requirements: Professional development for both core teachers and small-group instructors (three days in total)
Professional development workbooks and a Leadership Guide
target_learners: struggling first grade readers
target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills, vocabulary, and comprehension aligned with the Common Core State Standards
examples: In the studied program, all students received 90 minutes of core reading instruction and 30 minutes of Tier 2 instruction, with Tier 2 preteaching the core content.
key_sources: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research
citation: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research
title: Match sample definitions and analysis methods to the clustered design
description: Among the practical steps the article recommends for meeting evidence and accountability demands are "identifying appropriate sample definitions and analysis methods." In a clustered design this means defining the school and student samples deliberately and using analysis methods appropriate to clustered data, two of the six decisions the review identifies. The principle directs researchers to treat sampling and analysis as design decisions to be made together, not as afterthoughts.
requirements: Researchers must define school and student samples and choose analysis methods suited to clustered data
target_learners: school health researchers
target_learning_goals: valid analysis of cluster randomized trial data
examples: The review lists definition of the school and student samples and analysis methods as decisions (4) and (6) respectively.
key_sources: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation
citation: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Align analytic assumptions across methods when comparing impact estimation approaches
description: When evaluating whether choice of impact estimation method matters, the article indicates analysts should align the underlying analytic assumptions across the methods being compared. It notes the design- and model-based methods are most similar "when the underlying analytic assumptions (such as the weights used to aggregate clusters and blocks) are aligned". This makes method comparisons interpretable rather than confounded by differing weighting choices.
requirements: Access to the same RCT data across methods, with the ability to specify matching aggregation weights for clusters and blocks
constraints: Similarity of findings depends on the assumptions being aligned; the article does not claim equivalence when they differ
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators analyzing RCT impact data
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation and comparison of intervention impacts in education evaluations
examples: The study re-analyzed nine past education RCTs, estimating impacts with design-based, HLM, and robust standard error methods and comparing the resulting estimates and significance levels.
key_sources: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report
citation: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Allow sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation in partnership-based family engagement initiatives
description: Among the formative findings on the viability of leveraging public-private partnerships, the report identifies "the importance of (1) allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation." This principle directs funders, communities, and organizations to budget adequate transition time between planning and implementation phases of family engagement initiatives.
requirements: A public-private partnership structure supporting family engagement, moving from a planning phase into implementation.
target_learners: Low-income immigrant children from birth through age 8 and their families
target_learning_goals: Family engagement capacity building
examples: The report lists allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation as the first of six formative findings from FEIP grantees' implementation experiences.
key_sources: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/feip

article_title: Making Sense out of Incentives
citation: NO AUTHOR LINE. (2018). Incentive-Based Approaches to Improving Attendance. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk (JESPAR). https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/cjep20
title: Align incentive design with the nature of specific attendance barriers
description: The article recommends that incentive design begin with diagnosis: policymakers and practitioners need guidance on "how to design incentives in ways that align with the nature of specific attendance barriers and problems." Because attendance barriers differ, a single incentive design will not fit every school's situation.
requirements: Practitioners must first identify the specific attendance barriers and problems their students face before choosing or designing incentives
constraints: The article notes varied levels of success when incentives are employed without such alignment
target_learners: chronically absent students in pre-K to grade 12
target_learning_goals: improving attendance
examples: The framework prompts schools to decide whether incentives are an appropriate intervention for their particular attendance problem before implementing one

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Align new district initiatives to an existing Portrait and Learning Pathway rather than adding new programs
description: The article recommends that, with an Integrated Learning Pathway in place, "each new learning priority—whether it be computational thinking, social-emotional learning, artificial intelligence, or another—can be aligned to the Skill Sets and Practices already present in the district's Portrait." This lets educators see how initiatives relate to one another and to existing teaching, identifies where relevant Practices already exist, and removes the burden from individual teachers of figuring out each new initiative, supporting equity through consistency. The authors suggest this weaving into shared priorities may alleviate "Initiative Fatigue."
requirements: An existing district Portrait and a developed Integrated Learning Pathway
constraints: The article notes this addresses curricular integration only; whole-child pedagogical approaches and competency-based rubrics are left to forthcoming work
target_learners: K-12 students in districts adopting multiple initiatives
target_learning_goals: Coherent alignment of district initiatives to graduate skill outcomes
examples: Indian Prairie SD used its Portrait to align computational thinking and is next aligning AI literacy skills to the same framework, mapping AI evaluation categories to Portrait Skill Sets
key_sources: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205

article_title: Centering Wellbeing: Advancing Social Emotional Learning for All
citation: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177
title: Align professional learning initiatives with district leadership priorities and commitments to move ideas into action
description: The report identifies strategic alignment between a working group's focus and district leadership commitments as the first of three readiness factors accelerating implementation. Leaders who joined with clear aims—expanding SEL resources for deaf students, deepening existing wellness work, or advancing a superintendent's vision—moved from idea to action, which the report notes requires "commitment, effort, and—almost always—dedicated time and financial resources."
requirements: Dedicated time and financial resources, since moving from idea to action requires commitment, effort, and almost always dedicated time and financial resources
target_learners: district and school leaders
educators
target_learning_goals: strengthening SEL and wellbeing supports system-wide
examples: Dr. Tanner joined the working group specifically to expand adaptable SEL resources for deaf students; Dr. Moore built on existing district work to win wellness-center funding; Suffern's wellbeing focus was part of the superintendent's vision.

article_title: Structuring Out-of-School Time to Improve Academic Achievement
citation: Beckett, M., Borman, G., Capizzano, J., Parsley, D., Ross, S., Schirm, A., & Taylor, J. (2009). Structuring out-of-school time to improve academic achievement: A practice guide (NCEE #2009-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Align the OST program academically with the school day
description: OST programs and schools share the mission of helping students succeed, and the panel holds that "academic alignment with the school day is necessary for OST programs to improve academic performance." Alignment is achieved through OST program coordinators and designated school-based coordinators who maintain ongoing communication, align OST activities with state and local content standards and the school curriculum, and coordinate staffing. Tools include a logbook carried between classroom teachers and OST instructors sharing homework assignments, topics covered, and useful instructional strategies.
requirements: An OST program coordinator who maintains regular communication with school staff
A designated school staff person to coordinate communication with OST programs
Identification of school-based goals and learning objectives to connect OST instruction to school instruction
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low; no study tested its effectiveness individually, only in combination with other OST program components
target_learners: elementary and middle school students in school-based OST programs in low-income, high-needs communities
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in school-day content areas
examples: Coordinators can develop a logbook students carry back and forth daily to share information about OST activities with classroom teachers, and arrange for OST instructors to periodically attend common planning periods with classroom teachers.
key_sources: Beckett, M., Borman, G., Capizzano, J., Parsley, D., Ross, S., Schirm, A., & Taylor, J. (2009). article_title: Designing and Delivering Career Pathways at Community Colleges
citation: Cotner, H., Bragg, D., Cheng, I., Costelloe, S., Freeman, B., Goold, G., Heiser, E., Lemire, S., Miller, D.G., Porowski, A., Van Noy, M., & Yadav, E. (2021). Designing and delivering career pathways at community colleges: A practice guide for educators (WWC 2021007). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Align career pathways to regional industry needs using labor market information and employer input
description: The panel recommends that community colleges assess regional industry demand before designing pathways so that training leads to in-demand, family-sustaining occupations. Labor market information identifies growing occupations, wage levels, and advancement opportunities, and employers should review it collaboratively with colleges. As the guide states, "community colleges should assess and identify regional industry needs to ensure the pathways will provide students with the occupational skills and knowledge that employers demand."
requirements: Collaboration with employers and industry partners to review labor market information
Dedicated time for continuous program alignment work
constraints: The specific questions for reviewing labor market information are examples that can be modified to local needs and contexts

target_learning_goals: Occupational skills and knowledge aligned with employer demand
Employment in in-demand industries
examples: A training gap analysis matrix organizes training content, delivery models, and length by lower, middle, and higher skill occupations

article_title: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models
citation: Soland, J., Thum, Y.M., & King, G. (2019). Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models: Evidence and implications from a longitudinal study. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org
title: Policymakers should examine whether short-term growth accountability aligns with long-term goals like college and career readiness
description: Because school effectiveness estimates are highly sensitive to the timespan over which growth is measured, the article recommends that policymakers openly discuss how schools should be held accountable for long-term objectives. It argues policymakers "may need to ask themselves whether accountability policies based on short-term growth are creating incentives that jibe with their broader goal of college and career readiness," noting the current emphasis may be producing unintended consequences relative to long-term goals.
requirements: Growth estimates computed over multiple timespans so their sensitivity can be assessed
Awareness of the .90 correlation threshold below which accountability determinations are likely to change
constraints: The study could not estimate school contributions to growth between Kindergarten and 12th grade, only all tested elementary grades
Findings come from one state using a low-stakes assessment, so generalization is limited
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: Long-term outcomes such as college and career readiness and closing achievement gaps
examples: The article compared school effectiveness estimates from a single year, three years, and five years of data for 570 schools using the CP model
key_sources: Soland, J., Thum, Y.M., & King, G. (2019). Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models: Evidence and implications from a longitudinal study. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/reconciling-long-term-education-policy-goals-with-short-term-school-accountability-models-paper/

article_title: Systems Alignment and Coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's Early Care and Education System
citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Alignment and coherence framework with six interrelated domains for system improvement
description: The report defines alignment as "all policies, practices, processes, and roles in a system working together in similar or consistent ways" and coherence as integration that mutually reinforces shared understanding and progress toward a clear vision. It organizes the features of alignment and coherence along six interrelated domains—goals, funding and policies, strategic communication, interest holder engagement, capacity building, and data use—situated within a five-step data-driven continuous improvement process and technical and adaptive approaches to change. Alignment can be internal, horizontal, or vertical.
requirements: A shared vision and theory of change established as the first step of the continuous improvement process
Inventory of whole-person initiatives and analysis of interrelationships before creating an action plan
constraints: The framework is presented for child-, youth-, and family-serving systems, applied here to early care and learning in Alameda County
target_learners: Young children from birth through age 12 and their families in Alameda County early care and learning systems
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness and healthy learning and development through aligned, coherent early childhood systems
examples: The report applies the six domains to structure its analysis of First 5 Alameda's approach and opportunities for Measure C and the Oakland Children's Initiative
key_sources: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673491

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Align tutoring implementation with evidence-based dosage recommendations before launch
description: Because impacts appeared only when students approached the intended dosage, the report recommends that districts plan for sufficient time, stability, and support before adopting high-dosage tutoring. It states "it is important for districts to align their tutoring implementation with evidence-based dosage recommendations to ensure that sufficient time, stability, and support are available for the tutoring implementation," and that providers such as Air Tutors should ensure districts and schools are aware of dosage recommendations so students experience positive impacts.
requirements: District awareness of the program's recommended dosage (for Air Tutors, 30 hours via four to five 45-minute sessions weekly over 10 weeks)
constraints: In this evaluation, budget limitations, scheduling challenges, frequent cancellations, and delayed starts prevented District B from delivering the intended dosage
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students in high-dosage math tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: Math achievement gains from tutoring delivered at the intended dosage
examples: District A scheduled tutoring so that 93 percent of participants reached the 24-hour threshold, while District B's budget cuts and cancellations left 62 percent of participants at 15 or fewer hours
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673538

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Align edtech procurement with district needs and strategic priorities using specialized AI evaluation criteria
description: The article recommends that districts plan AI-enabled edtech purchases through formal, cross-functional processes rather than reacting to sales pitches. It states that "AI-enabled tools require specialized evaluation criteria that address unique considerations, including algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, data privacy implications, and the need for ongoing monitoring of AI system performance and outputs." Recommendations include cross-functional teams, formal planning processes, and data-driven needs assessments.
requirements: Cross-functional collaboration so technical requirements and pedagogical objectives are both met
Data-driven needs assessments
constraints: Applies to AI-enabled tools, which the article says need specialized criteria beyond general edtech evaluation
target_learners: District administrators and procurement teams
target_learning_goals: Selecting AI-enabled edtech that aligns with learning objectives
examples: The vision and planning phase lists key challenges of siloed processes, lack of clear vision, and reliance on sales pitches
key_sources: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Align performance-based assessments with standards, curriculum, and instruction
description: The report's first cross-state lesson is that "Intentional work should be done to align performance-based assessments with standards, curriculum, and instruction." Interviewees in every state emphasized embedding performance assessments in classroom curriculum and instruction so they evaluate "content and standards together using authentic, student-centered methods." Misalignment risks assessments being perceived as add-on activities for teachers and feeling jarring to students.
requirements: Performance assessments should be embedded in the classroom's curriculum and instruction and aligned with state standards, including embedded skills such as communication and collaboration.
constraints: Interviewees cautioned that misalignment between assessment and curriculum could make the assessments feel like add-on activities for teachers and jarring to students.
target_learners: K-12 students in states implementing performance-based graduation or classroom assessment options
target_learning_goals: Demonstration of mastery of content standards and transferable or essential skills
examples: State interviewees advised incorporating both content and skills into the performance assessment process, noting content is the vehicle through which students demonstrate essential skills.
key_sources: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633310

article_title: State Preschool in a Mixed Delivery System: Lessons from Five States
citation: Garver, K., Weisenfeld, G. G., Connors-Tadros, L., Hodges, K., Melnick, H., & Plasencia, S. (2023). State preschool in a mixed delivery system: Lessons from five states. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/387.446
title: Establish strong program standards aligned across LEA and non-LEA settings so all children receive high-quality preschool experiences
description: The report's first recommendation holds that states operating mixed delivery preschool should set the same quality standards for every provider setting. The case study states "have high quality standards that are aligned across LEAs and non-LEAs to ensure that families have access to quality care in a variety of settings," including shared curriculum, class size, ratio, professional development, and child assessment requirements. The report argues this alignment supports equitable access to quality regardless of setting.
requirements: Funding and oversight structures must enable all settings to meet the shared standards, including coaching and professional development access for non-LEAs
constraints: The report notes the cost of meeting high quality standards can vary across setting, so funding levels must allow providers in all settings to meet them
target_learners: Children enrolled in state-funded preschool in LEA and non-LEA settings
target_learning_goals: Consistent access to high-quality preschool learning environments
examples: All five case study states require an evidence-based curriculum, class size of 20 or less, and at least a 1:10 teacher-to-child ratio in both LEA and non-LEA settings
key_sources: Garver, K., Weisenfeld, G. G., Connors-Tadros, L., Hodges, K., Melnick, H., & Plasencia, S. (2023). State preschool in a mixed delivery system: Lessons from five states. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/387.446

article_title: One-Shot Deal? Students' Perceptions of Assessment and Course Placement in California's Community Colleges
citation: Venezia, A., Bracco, K. R., & Nodine, T. (2010). One-shot deal? Students' perceptions of assessment and course placement in California's community colleges. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: High schools and community colleges should align efforts toward informing and preparing students well before placement
description: The report's central recommendation is to replace the one-day, arrival-time placement experience with "a more seamless, longer-lasting set of processes wherein high schools and community colleges align their efforts toward informing and preparing students." Students should learn requirements early in high school so they can master needed knowledge, skills, and cognitive strategies, and should have ways to gauge their preparation and get support in both high school and college. The principle responds directly to findings that students arrive knowing next to nothing about what to expect.
requirements: Coordination between K-12 and postsecondary systems despite the structural divide between them
Communication to students about readiness requirements early in their high school years
constraints: The report states improvements will be extremely challenging to implement in the environment of budgetary crisis and program instability, and what students most want is more one-on-one counselor time, an expensive intervention
target_learners: Incoming community college students, particularly recent high school graduates
target_learning_goals: College readiness in English and mathematics and informed navigation of assessment and placement
examples: The report also recommends efficiencies such as a common assessment system and centralized Assessment Warehouse, and notes 97 percent of surveyed colleges offer student success courses teaching study skills and college habits of mind.
key_sources: Venezia, A., Bracco, K. R., & Nodine, T. (2010). One-shot deal? Students' perceptions of assessment and course placement in California's community colleges. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566386

article_title: Examination of Data Usability Options for Assessing Eligibility for Higher Education in California
citation: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Before using CALPADS course records for eligibility studies, align CALPADS A-G categorization with UC/CSU categorization for each year and school
description: The report recommends reviewing how courses are categorized into A-G categories in CALPADS so that categorization matches what the UC/CSU systems use. It states that "A review of the categorization of courses into A-G categories in CALPADS so that it matches, for each year and school, the categorization used by the UC/CSU system would solve that challenge," addressing the very low elective (G) matching rate. This recommendation follows directly from the alignment analyses showing G-course non-alignment.
requirements: Access to CALPADS course records with A-G indicators and course labels
Knowledge of the UC/CSU categorization used for each year and school
constraints: Applies to the elective (G) categorization problem the report identified; the report notes 2011-2015 CALPADS data may preclude estimating 2015 graduate eligibility rates
target_learners: California public high school students being assessed for UC/CSU eligibility
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of A-G course completion for higher education eligibility
examples: The report's alignment tables (Tables 3-12) showed G-course exact alignment of only about 20-30% while other A-G areas reached 70-87%
key_sources: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED592524

article_title: AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education -- A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory
citation: Sushan Adhikari. (2026). AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education — A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14572
title: AlgoRAG: a five-stage RAG pipeline for theoretical computer science education
description: AlgoRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation system coupling DeepSeek V3 with a curated TCS knowledge base. Its "five-stage pipeline" performs query analysis with mathematical entity recognition, hybrid dense-and-sparse retrieval, pedagogical re-ranking on educational utility, context-grounded generation with structured prompt templates, and post-processing that normalizes inline mathematics and formats numbered proof steps. It is implemented in Python with sentence-transformers embeddings, ChromaDB vector storage, and a released evaluation harness.
requirements: A curated domain-specific knowledge base and a generation model with sufficient multi-step mathematical-reasoning performance (the article found locally-hosted Llama 2 and Mistral insufficient)
constraints: Results depend on the DeepSeek V3 API, which introduces external latency and availability constraints; at 38.0 s per query it suits asynchronous study rather than real-time classroom interaction
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate theoretical computer science students
target_learning_goals: algorithm analysis
complexity theory
formal proof techniques and asymptotic reasoning
examples: Evaluated on 179 exam-style questions spanning asymptotic analysis, recurrence relations, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, NP-completeness, sorting, and divide-and-conquer

title: Curated TCS knowledge base with 847 lecture slides, 312 practice problems, 156 proof templates, and 89 complexity worksheets

Items are tagged with topic, difficulty, and concept keywords, and a multi-dimensional index plus a lightweight CS knowledge graph link algorithm names to complexity classes so paraphrased queries reach conceptually related material.
requirements: Tagging of every item with topic, difficulty level, and concept keywords, and a multi-dimensional index capturing conceptual associations
constraints: Assembled from publicly available resources and may have coverage gaps for newer algorithmic results
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate theoretical computer science students
target_learning_goals: algorithm analysis and complexity theory across the full undergraduate–graduate TCS curriculum
examples: A query about recursion trees surfaces material on recurrence relations and divide-and-conquer even if terminology differs

article_title: Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment
citation: Chen C and Liu T (2026) Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment. Front. Psychol. 17:1867463. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1867463
title: Align teacher feedback with automated feedback in timing and individuation to support planning and emotional regulation
description: The article recommends that teacher feedback be aligned with automated feedback "in timing and individuation" so that the two sources jointly support the SRL phases automated scoring leaves untouched. Automated scores sustain deliberate practice during execution, but planning and emotional regulation need human scaffolding that is timely and individualized. The recommendation arises from the finding that students rarely analyzed why errors occurred and that emotional responses to scores diverged.
requirements: Instructors must have capacity to provide feedback that matches the immediacy and individualization of automated scores
constraints: The article notes instructor supply limits timely, substantive feedback to every student on every after-class exercise in conventional settings
target_learners: student interpreters (MTI/undergraduate translation and interpreting majors)
target_learning_goals: interpreting performance
self-regulated learning, especially planning and emotional regulation
examples: Over 14 weeks the experimental group used the Yunyi system for after-class tasks while both groups received collective instructor feedback in the following week's class

article_title: When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education
citation: Chen Y (2026) When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education. Front. Psychol. 17:1955192. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955192
title: Universities should align GAI commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices while helping students develop alternative coping routes
description: The article's practical implication is that institutional advocacy for generative AI must be matched by consistent implementation, and that students should simultaneously be supported in developing alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty. As the article puts it, "Universities should align GAI commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices while helping students develop alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty." The principle rests on the finding that inconsistency evokes both hindrance and challenge appraisals with opposing engagement consequences.
requirements: Institutions must make public GAI commitments operational in course arrangements, instructor practices, resource support, and assessment standards
constraints: The findings are associational and specific to GAI-supported art education in Chinese higher education institutions
target_learners: art students in higher education using GAI tools
target_learning_goals: maintaining creative process engagement under uncertain institutional AI implementation
examples: The article recommends aligning commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices and helping students develop alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty.

article_title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
citation: Rismanchian, S., Uzun, H., Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Kurd-Misto, E. (2026). Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21629
title: ALEKS and ALEKS PPL behavioral trace datasets for studying AI-era learning behavior
description: The study builds on two large log datasets from ALEKS, an adaptive mathematics learning and assessment platform built on knowledge space theory: "3.2 million ALEKS learning interactions for investigating time-on-task, complemented by 12.2 million ALEKS PPL placement-assessment response times for examining proctoring and learning outcomes". The learning panel spans Grade 5 through College Algebra over 2015 Q3–2025 Q3; the PPL panel covers more than 400 US institutions, with proctored and non-proctored sessions and randomly assigned extra retention items.
requirements: Analysis requires item-level AI-susceptibility classification, validated by an author on 100 randomly selected items with an LLM classifier replicating labels at 86% agreement (Cohen's κ= 0.79)
constraints: The article notes ALEKS did not integrate generative-AI tutoring or hints post-ChatGPT, so shifts reflect student behavior outside the platform; anonymized data is available only upon request
target_learners: Grade 5 through college mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Measuring time-on-task, response times, and retention in mathematics
examples: The retention analysis restricted to randomly assigned extra questions appearing in 1 out of every 30 PPL session items, assigned independently of the adaptive algorithm

article_title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: Algorithmic colonialingualism: GenAI's standard-English-based algorithmic systems exclude the linguistic repertoires of marginalised speakers
description: Algorithmic colonialingualism is a concept proposed by contributor Sender Dovchin to name how GenAI can re-colonise language: "the algorithmic system of GenAI is based on standard English varieties, while most varieties of world Englishes are not often reflected". The article gives Aboriginal English spoken by First Nations people in Australia as an unreflected example, and notes AI systems are not designed to handle translanguaging, the fluid movement between linguistic and semiotic repertoires. The concept frames GenAI as a double-edged sword that risks excluding marginalised speakers from AI design and functionality.
requirements: Analysis of GenAI's linguistic inclusivity must attend to which varieties are represented in training data and system design
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual framing from one contributor's afterword, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: Academic writers and publishers, especially scholars from Indigenous, migrant, and Global South backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Critical awareness of linguistic bias in GenAI-mediated academic writing
examples: Dovchin's analysis of translanguaging data showing AI systems cannot accommodate flexible hybrid practices

article_title: Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach
citation: McCorkle, S. (2025). Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach. International Journal of Designs for Learning, 16(2), 96–110. https://doi.org/10.14434/ijdl.v16i2.41058
title: Aligned Generative AI Course Policy framework for deciding allowed and unallowed GenAI use per task
description: The article presents an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy as a design framework in which "the allowed and unallowed uses of GenAI tools are described in a transparent manner for students." Rather than a blanket course-wide rule, the framework aligns each GenAI permission decision with what the instructor actually assesses for each student task. It works by decomposing the course into its constituent student tasks, classifying each as assessed or as an intermediate step, and matching each task to a GenAI workforce competency before deciding whether assessment or competency-building takes priority.
requirements: The instructor must analyze student tasks by creating an inventory of each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning
constraints: The framework is presented as a design case describing one course policy design, not as a tested intervention
target_learners: higher education students in courses with GenAI tools available
target_learning_goals: transparent and equitable use of generative AI tools in coursework
emerging GenAI workforce competencies
examples: The design case documents the policy being designed for a course whose student tasks were inventoried step by step toward finished products of learning

description: The article's forward-looking design recommendation is that the framework should inform instructional design in higher education. The abstract states: "The article concludes by illustrating how the framework may inform instructional design that aligns AI use with meaningful engagement in disciplinary tasks in higher education." The principle directs designers to use the framework's cognitive and motivational mechanisms to structure AI integration that supports thinking rather than bypassing it.

constraints: Illustrative rather than empirically validated; framed as a possibility ("may inform")

target_learning_goals: Meaningful disciplinary engagement supported by generative AI
examples: The article concludes by illustrating how the framework may inform instructional design aligning AI use with meaningful engagement in disciplinary tasks

article_title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Align robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than prioritizing anthropomorphic appearance when deploying educational robots
description: The article recommends that educational robot design and deployment focus on matching what robots do to interaction goals instead of relying on looks. It states that "designers of educational robots should prioritize aligning robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than focusing primarily on anthropomorphic appearance". Robots may be accepted as instructional guides regardless of embodiment, while emotionally sensitive tasks need extra design work such as transparency, privacy assurances, or enhanced socio-emotional behaviors.
requirements: Robots must be positioned within educational workflows according to task demands, with behavioral or relational mechanisms added before use in emotionally sensitive interactions
constraints: Findings come from video-based, script-controlled short-term evaluations with a homogeneous sample of Greek undergraduate future educators; the article notes video-mediation can mitigate appearance effects and calls for testing real-time, longitudinal, and broader-population interactions
target_learners: undergraduate future educators (pre-service teachers)
target_learning_goals: trust in socially assistive robots across educational tasks (teaching, procedural instruction, personal-information discussion)
examples: In the experiment, all three robots delivered identical scripts across teaching, instruction, and personal-information tasks, and trust followed task type (T2 > T1 > T3) while robot type showed no meaningful effect

article_title: 'Why SuaCode?": Understanding African Students'' Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course'
citation: Michael Addo, Nana Maryam Munagah, Victor Kumbol, Judith Uchidiuno, and George Boateng. (2026). “Why SuaCode?”: Understanding African Students’ Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22940
title: Design programming MOOCs for African students around their interests and goals rather than relying on free, accessible content alone to drive enrollment
description: The article recommends that insights into students' motivations "can inform the design of MOOC content and assessments to align with students' interests." Because SuaCode students enrolled primarily for intrinsic reasons tied to interest and personal goals, while free and accessible content ranked low (4%) as a motivator, designers of programming MOOCs targeted at African students should foreground course theme and applicability to learners' goals rather than assuming no-cost access suffices to attract enrollees.
requirements: Understanding of the target students' motivations for enrolling, gathered for example via open-ended response surveys
constraints: The authors note this trend suggests accessible content alone may not suffice "without accounting for other factors"; the finding is from a preliminary analysis of one course's respondents

High school, university, and recent-graduate learners in Africa and the diaspora
target_learning_goals: Computer programming skills
Sustained engagement and persistence in online coding courses
examples: SuaCode's enrollment was driven primarily by students' interest in the program's theme and its applicability to their goals, even though the course is freely accessible via smartphones

title: Align GenAI integration with strategic learning outcomes to support coherent and sustainable adoption
description: The article's guiding principle for business educators is that GenAI adoption should be designed through constructive alignment: tools and activities are chosen so that they serve the module's intended learning outcomes rather than being adopted ad hoc. The authors state the study offers "practical guidance for aligning GenAI with strategic learning outcomes, supporting more coherent and sustainable adoption in business higher education". article_title: The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study
citation: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069
title: Align agent knowledge configuration with feedback delivery style when designing AI feedback scaffolding
description: The article argues from a scaffolding perspective that agent type and feedback style jointly constitute AI feedback scaffolding: "the effect of AI feedback depends not only on agent type or feedback style alone, but on how a specific agent type and feedback style jointly constitute scaffolding that matches learners' current needs." Designers should therefore choose the knowledge configuration and delivery style as a matched pair rather than optimizing each independently, since the customized agent's outcome advantage appeared only under directive feedback.
requirements: Explicit consideration of both the agent's knowledge sources and its feedback delivery style at design time
constraints: The customized-agent advantage under directive feedback was observed for short-term task improvement in open-ended instructional design tasks with postgraduate students, in a fixed feedback-style sequence

target_learning_goals: Effective use of AI-generated feedback
Short-term task improvement
examples: In the experiment, all participants received Socratic feedback in Week 1 and directive feedback in Week 2 under their assigned agent type

citation: Marcin Jukiewicz. (2025). A systematic comparison of Large Language Models for automated assignment assessment in programming education: Exploring the importance of architecture and vendor. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26483
title: Align LLM grader selection with pedagogical goals and maintain human oversight
description: Because LLMs exhibit distinct grading philosophies and only moderate agreement with human teachers, the article argues that "the choice of model for educational deployment is not neutral". citation: Yim, K.-H.; Lui, M. Y. (2026). Supporting Undergraduate Students' Learning in Practical Chemistry Courses through AI-Supported Experimental Design. Journal of Chemical Education. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jchemed.5c01311
title: Almeida Bauer Zytkuewisz rubric for characterizing levels of inquiry in undergraduate laboratories
description: A rubric that differentiates laboratory activities into six levels (originally five, recently updated) based on six characteristics: problem/question, theory/background, procedure/design, result/analysis, results communication, and conclusions. The level of inquiry is determined by the amount of information provided to students. Level 3 authentic inquiry provides no information for any characteristic and is considered impractical in undergraduate courses due to difficulty, complexity, safety risks, and students' limited technical expertise. This article's activity was designed to align with Level 3.
requirements: Characterization of laboratory activities across six information-provision dimensions
constraints: Level 3 authentic inquiry is often considered impractical in undergraduate laboratory courses due to inherent difficulty, complexity, safety risks, and students' lack of technical expertise
target_learners: undergraduate laboratory students
target_learning_goals: characterizing inquiry levels in laboratory course design
examples: The article's lab manual design project aligned with Level 3 by providing six broad topics without predefined problems or theoretical backgrounds

article_title: Algorithm Aversion: People Erroneously Avoid Algorithms after Seeing Them Err
citation: Berkeley J. Dietvorst, Joseph P. Simmons, and Cade Massey. (2014). Algorithm Aversion: People Erroneously Avoid Algorithms After Seeing Them Err. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000033
title: Algorithm aversion: greater intolerance for error from algorithms than from humans
description: The article names and substantively describes algorithm aversion, the tendency to avoid algorithmic forecasters in favor of inferior human forecasters. It proposes a mechanism: people "more quickly lose confidence in algorithmic than human forecasters after seeing them make the same mistake," so seeing an algorithm perform and err increases aversion even when the algorithm outperforms. The construct frames the five studies, in which experience with the forecaster is manipulated before participants bet on forecasts.
requirements: Algorithms must occasionally err visibly for the aversion to arise; without experience with the algorithm, participants often choose it
constraints: The article notes its studies cannot say whether the effect would persist if algorithms were many times more accurate than humans than the advantage tested here
target_learners: adult forecasters and decision makers choosing between human and algorithmic judgment
target_learning_goals: choosing between human and statistical forecasting methods when making predictions
examples: In five studies, participants forecast MBA applicants' success or U.S. states' airline-passenger ranks and chose whether to tie incentives to the model's or a human's forecasts

article_title: Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs
citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Always report effect sizes, specify the standardizer used, report generalized eta squared for ANOVAs, and interpret effect sizes rather than relying on Cohen's benchmarks
description: The article's discussion sets four reporting practices for cumulative science: effect sizes should always be reported; for Cohen's d the standardizer must be specified, for example with subscripts (ds, dz, drm, dav); for ANOVAs, generalized eta squared should be reported instead of or in addition to partial eta squared; and effect sizes should be interpreted by comparison with other effects in the literature or via the common language effect size rather than the benchmarks provided by Cohen (1988).
requirements: Reporting effect sizes based on Cohen's d requires specifying which standardizer is used
constraints: The article limits its scope to effect sizes for standardized mean differences in t-tests and ANOVAs, not all research designs
target_learners: researchers planning and reporting experimental studies
target_learning_goals: transparent reporting of effect magnitudes
facilitating meta-analyses and power analyses
examples: The article's worked example reports Hedges's gs = 1.08 with means, SDs, t-value, and 95% CI, and adds a common language effect size interpretation that the preference for Movie 1 is 79%

study planning
goal attainment in standards-linked academic work

article_title: Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later
citation: W. Lewis Johnson & James C. Lester. (2015). Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0065-9
title: Alelo VCAT Virtual Cultural Awareness Trainers with multi-role Virtual Coach
description: VCATs are training systems in which learners acquire knowledge about other cultures and apply it in simulated encounters with virtual role-players, with advice and feedback from a Virtual Coach. The Virtual Coach shifts realization across the course: animated character at the start, fading to a less obtrusive presence, narrator as a disembodied voice, off-screen coach during role-plays popping up as a static image, and fading away entirely at the end so learners demonstrate the task unassisted. VCATs have been developed for over 80 countries and over 50,000 trainees have taken VCAT courses, providing evidence about which agent realizations fit which roles.
requirements: The agent's role must be clear to learners; the authors found that an unclear role can have a negative effect on learning effectiveness, as when one agent played both teammate and coach in Tactical Iraqi
constraints: For virtual role-players there are very few instances in which it makes sense for them to be disembodied voices

article_title: Learning to write letters: Examination of student and letter factors
citation: Puranik Cynthia S., Petscher Yaacov, Lonigan Christopher J. (2014). Learning to Write Letters: Examination of Student and Letter Factors. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2014.07.009
title: Introduce the same letters for teaching letter names and for letter writing
description: The article's instructional implication is that because letter-name knowledge contributed substantially to letter-writing skills, "it might be beneficial to introduce the same letters for teaching letter names and for letter writing." This follows from the finding that knowing a letter's name sharply raised the probability of writing it correctly for 4- and 5-year-olds. The authors caution that such decisions require experimental confirmation, including whether teaching writing is more effective when students already know the letter names.

constraints: The authors state this recommendation is provisional and can be made only after experimental questions are addressed

letter-name knowledge

citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4

citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Align performance-review media such as video with instructional aims, facilitator expertise, and the emotional climate of training
description: The editorial draws the broader lesson from the video-debriefing studies that "media are not neutral – they must be aligned with instructional aims, facilitator expertise, and the emotional climate of training". Performance-review tools such as video not only extend reflection but also impose new design responsibilities, making tools instructional decisions rather than neutral add-ons.

article_title: Observational learning from animated models: effects of studying–practicing alternation and illusion of control on transfer
citation: Pieter Wouters, Fred Paas, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2008). Observational learning from animated models: effects of studying–practicing alternation and illusion of control on transfer. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9079-0
title: When providing learner control in a learning environment, ensure learners' expectations of control match the control they can actually exert
description: The article concludes that "merely providing learner control in a learning context without considering the expectations of learners regarding the control can have a negative effect on learning". Designers of responsive learning environments, which the authors note can be laborious and relatively expensive to develop, must take into account how they deal with the expectations of the learners who will use them, because a mismatch between expected and actual control wastes cognitive capacity on activities that do not contribute to learning.
requirements: The learning environment must be responsive to learner choices so that relevant changes in instruction result from learners' decisions
constraints: Demonstrated for probability calculation instruction with pre-university pupils who already had some prior knowledge; immediate testing only, so long-term effects are unknown

target_learning_goals: transfer of problem-solving procedures in probability calculation
examples: In the experiment, learners in no-illusion conditions pressed meaningfully named buttons that presented the selected problem, while illusion-of-control learners pressed meaninglessly named buttons with problems always presented in a fixed order

article_title: From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary Learning
citation: Xiaoxuan Li · Julia Chatain · Fan Wang · Manu Kapur. (2026). From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10194-9
title: Design embodied vocabulary activities so learners' movements meaningfully align with target word meanings
description: The meta-analysis identifies movement-meaning congruency as the most robust moderator of embodied vocabulary learning: movements that transparently represent the semantic meaning of the target word (e.g., miming jumping when learning the verb jump) yield larger effects than arbitrary movements in both between- and within-subject designs. The authors conclude that "semantic alignment between movement and target word meanings is a key design feature of embodied vocabulary learning" and that congruency "should be considered as a key factor when developing embodied learning interventions."
requirements: Bodily actions must be physically performed by the learners themselves, not by teachers, robots, or pedagogical agents
constraints: The pooled effects may overestimate the true magnitude due to detected publication bias
target_learners: preschool children
primary school students
high school students
college students
adult language learners
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
second and foreign language word learning
examples: In the included studies, congruent conditions included producing iconic gestures (Tellier, 2008) and acting out word meanings with full-body movements (Toumpaniari et al., 2015), whereas non-congruent conditions involved arbitrary hand movements or repetitive tapping patterns

citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Align the chosen PE teaching model with the curriculum's intended student outcomes
description: The review endorses the suggestion that specific teaching models should be selected to emphasize particular student outcomes depending on curriculum aims: "specific models should be used to emphasize certain student outcomes, depending on the aims and objectives of the PE curriculum". Tactical skill, procedural knowledge and affective domains are accentuated in TGAs, while technical skill and declarative knowledge are emphasized more in TAs. The review notes it seems commonplace that PE teachers do not align appropriate models to curriculum goals, with most still featuring traditional teacher-centered models.

Teacher capacity to deliver the chosen model as intended
constraints: The review also reports complexity thinking suggests no one correct teaching model, indicating teachers adopt a range of pedagogical models

target_learning_goals: Matching pedagogy to intended outcomes across tactical, technical, cognitive and affective domains
examples: The review classifies outcomes into seven categories (tactical skill, skill execution, technical skill, affective, declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, physical activity) that different approaches emphasize differently

citation: Silla, E. M., Guba, T.-P., Rodrigues, A., Anisiobi, O. C., Scanniello, A., & Barbieri, C. A. (2026). A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10111-6
title: Taxonomy of algebraic thinking operationalizations: global measures versus specific facets
description: The review organizes algebra outcome measures into a taxonomy distinguishing global constructs from specific facets. It states that 'some studies focus on conceptual understanding of algebraic concepts, such as the equal sign, negative sign, variables, and exponents; this is often referred to as algebraic feature knowledge.' Other operationalizations include equation encoding, 'their ability to perceptually process and represent equation structures, components, and terms,' and equation-solving accuracy on linear equations. The review argues propensities 'may be differentially related to algebra understanding depending on the algebra outcome measure used.'
requirements: Studies must use a standalone performance measure of algebra specifically, not a general math measure or course grade.
constraints: The taxonomy was applied to U.S. studies of students in grades 6-12; college algebra was excluded as distinct from secondary education.
target_learners: U.S. middle and high school students (grades 6-12)
target_learning_goals: Algebraic thinking, including algebraic feature knowledge, equation encoding, and equation-solving
examples: Twelve of the 61 reviewed studies measured specific facets of algebra knowledge, with equation-solving and algebraic feature knowledge the most prevalent assessments.

description: The article argues that because perceived competence and skills influence each other at different speeds, both intervention design and longitudinal modeling must match the timescales of the processes targeted. The abstract states the findings "underscore the importance of aligning intervention strategies and model specifications with the timescales of the underlying psychological processes". article_title: Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Align gamification design with students' psychological needs, limiting excessive competition and prioritizing personal progress and cooperative tasks
description: The review concludes that gamification enhances motivation and engagement in mathematics "when designs are aligned with students’ needs, balancing competition with mastery and cooperation". Elements added superficially are unlikely to be effective; instead, mastery-oriented structures, gradual progression through increasing difficulty, individual progress indicators, and cooperative mechanics that foster relatedness are recommended. Educators should "limit excessive competition and prioritize personal progress and cooperative tasks that foster social interaction".
requirements: Designs must balance competition with mastery and cooperation, supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness
constraints: Competitive features can be motivating, but if overemphasized, they risk discouraging less competitive students; external rewards require careful use
target_learners: Secondary and higher education mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Sustaining motivation and engagement in mathematics
examples: The review reports that interventions combining gamification with interactive or narrative structures tended to increase participation and attention, and that cooperative mechanics fostered relatedness while balancing competition

article_title: The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn
citation: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2
title: Align assessment modality and knowledge types with the learning strategies under study when evaluating drawing to learn
description: The review argues that because drawing evokes nonverbal, pictorial processing, assessments should cover the modalities and knowledge types targeted in the learning phase. It recommends that "a variety of outcomes including retention, transfer, and inferential knowledge (see Cromley et al., 2020) should optimally be covered by an assessment when studying the learning strategy of drawing." Studies that aligned verbal and pictorial tests with all compared strategies allowed more differentiated and comparable conclusions.
requirements: Assessment batteries must include tests matching the modality of every learning strategy compared, including pictorial (drawing) tests alongside verbal tests.
constraints: The review notes some results suggest drawing can be effective beyond pictorial learning situations, so alignment alone does not guarantee detecting benefits.
target_learners: researchers and educators assessing drawing-based learning tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of drawing effects on retention, transfer, and inferential knowledge
examples: Schwamborn et al. (2010) and Schmeck et al. (2014) used transfer, retention, and drawing tests covering verbal and pictorial modalities, yielding differentiated results, whereas Bobek and Tversky (2016) used only verbal tests.

article_title: Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning
citation: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w
title: Align learning strategy choice with the instructional goal: induction versus memory consolidation
description: The article recommends that instructional decisions be guided by whether students are discovering a rule or strengthening one they already understand. For rule induction, teachers can "present varied worked examples and ask students to identify the underlying pattern to promote inductive learning through practice," or use varied problem solving with feedback. Once students can articulate and apply the rule, the goal shifts to consolidation, where retrieval practice such as short quizzes and cumulative review becomes especially effective.

Retrieval practice in the study was paired with corrective feedback, which the authors say likely supported rule induction
constraints: Under consolidation conditions, the article warns that introducing additional variability may impose unnecessary cognitive demands without benefit
Findings come from artificial language and mathematics rule-learning tasks with adults; ecological validity to authentic classrooms is untested
target_learners: school and adult learners acquiring rules or skills, e.g., in mathematics
target_learning_goals: rule induction and schema formation
retention and stable application of learned rules
examples: The article's mathematics example: students examine expressions such as 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6, 4(x + 5) = 4x + 20, and 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3 to induce the distributive property, then later retrieve and apply the rule via structurally similar problems

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Align reliable processes with the epistemic aims they are meant to achieve
description: The principle holds that strategies teachers select — rubrics, scoring guides, taxonomies, assessment formats — must align with the epistemic aims they are intended to serve. The article states: "Chinn et al. (2014) indicated that there must be alignment between the epistemic aim and the reliable process employed." For example, a single-point rubric better serves an aim of understanding student work, while a detailed analytic rubric better serves an aim of justifying grades to parents.
requirements: Teachers must identify their epistemic aim before selecting a reliable process, and evaluate whether required tools align with aims they hold
constraints: School curricula and policies often dictate the evaluation system teachers must implement, which may have been developed for an aim the teacher does not hold
target_learners: teachers
preservice teachers
target_learning_goals: selecting assessment tools and strategies that serve identified epistemic aims
examples: A teacher choosing between a single-point rubric and an analytic rubric depending on whether the aim is understanding students or justifying grades

citation: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv
title: Pair psychological mindset messages with visible structural flexibility ('aligned' interventions)
description: The article proposes aligned interventions that combine psychological messages with visible structural flexibility, so that growth-oriented messages are not delivered into settings that contradict them. It argues that instructional design choices matter because they provide credible evidence that the environment will adapt and that alternative pathways are treated as real in practice. The principle follows the wise-interventions insight that meaning shifts stick when the surrounding setting stops contradicting the new story.
requirements: Instructors and institutions must make flexibility concrete and credible, since persistence depends less on slogans about effort than on visible, reliable adaptation
constraints: Growth-mindset language delivered without corresponding changes in learning conditions can land as added pressure to push through when the real bottleneck is access, design, or institutional follow-through
target_learners: Disabled and neurodivergent learners
Students in settings with enduring structural constraints
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and persistence under constraint
examples: Structuring a lab into complementary roles when equipment demands exceed a student's fine-motor capacity, such as one student handling apparatus setup while another leads data logging and analysis

article_title: The elimination of Freshmen from the University of Texas.
citation: E. D. Jennings. (1911). The Elimination of Freshmen from the University of Texas. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=elimination+of+freshmen+from+the+university+of+texas
title: Close the high-school-to-university grading gap by raising university freshman ratings and lowering high-school senior ratings by about 10 per cent (one letter)

It argues the current break "tends to discourage him and to drive him out of school," and that closing "the unnatural and harmful breach between them" would reduce the large percentage of elimination.
