constraints: The article frames the 10 per cent, or one-letter, adjustment as an estimate tied to the observed 16 per cent gap and the two-thirds rating ratio, not as a tested optimum
target_learners: entering university freshmen
high-school senior classes
target_learning_goals: persistence through the first years of university study
fair and continuous assessment across the secondary-to-higher-education transition
examples: The article reports that the same students averaged 85 per cent in the last year of high school and 70 per cent at the university, and that reducing grades to arbitrary percentages again showed a difference of about 16 per cent between the two systems' standards.

gifted students
target_learning_goals: matching curriculum pace and depth to advanced learning needs

title: Use quick mass-administered alertness tests to inform borderline promotion versus non-promotion decisions

constraints: The diagnostic result is more reliable for subnormal than for supernormal pupils
Reading difficulties preclude extensive use below the fourth grade

target_learning_goals: Identifying retardation related to mental sluggishness and informing promotion decisions

article_title: The limits set to educational achievement by limited intelligence.
citation: Cobb, Margaret V. (1922). The Limits Set to Educational Achievement by Limited Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XIII, No. 8. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Limits+Set+to+Educational+Achievement+by+Limited+Intelligence
title: Conversion table relating median Army Alpha scores to median Stanford-Binet mental ages
description: The article builds a working table (Table III) pairing median Army Alpha scores from 175 down to 10 with median mental ages from 20-6 down to 9-6, so that its high school figures can be "expressed, so far as possible, both as Alpha scores, and in terms of the Stanford-Binet Scale." The table was made up after a study of the Army, Kohs-Proctor, Kansas State Normal School, and Doll norms, and the authors state it is far from being considered final. Examples of the pairings include Alpha 175 with MA 20-6, Alpha 130 with MA 17-6, and Alpha 65 with MA 14-6.

article_title: How the predictors of math achievement change over time: A longitudinal machine learning approach.
citation: Lavelle-Hill, R., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lichtenfeld, S., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Sakaki, M., Smith, G., & Murayama, K. (2024). How the Predictors of Math Achievement Change Over Time: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(8), 1383–1403. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000863
title: All-inclusive machine learning approach to modeling achievement predictors
description: The article coins an "all-inclusive approach": modeling the entire set of potential predictors, including their nonlinear and complex interactions, at once, rather than testing a small subset of predictors. Machine learning makes this feasible because regularization and out-of-sample evaluation protect against overfitting and multicollinearity that destabilize traditional regression with many predictors. The approach is applied to the PALMA longitudinal data with Elastic Net and Random Forest models, using a pipeline of training/test splitting, five-fold cross-validation, and SHAP-based variable importance for interpretation.
requirements: A large longitudinal data set containing an extensive set of predictor variables assessed consistently over time
Machine learning pipeline with cross-validation and out-of-sample testing to guard against overfitting
constraints: Variable importance measures are model- and method-dependent and should be interpreted with caution, ideally in combination with relevant theories
These measures are unlikely to reflect only the causal effects of the predictors on the outcome
The pipeline does not explicitly account for the hierarchical structure of students nested within classes
target_learners: secondary school students (Years 5–9)
target_learning_goals: predicting and understanding longitudinal change in mathematics achievement
examples: The article states: "the current paper takes a different approach: Analyzing all of the variables included in a large longitudinal data set to predict math achievement over time, which we coin an 'all-inclusive approach'"

article_title: Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals
citation: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w
title: WM-system account of neurofeedback transfer: alpha NF benefits tasks relying on the visuospatial sketchpad but not tasks relying on the phonological loop
description: The article proposes that contradictory outcomes of alpha NF studies arise because WM tasks engage different storage systems. "alpha activity tends to occur during tasks that require maintenance of simultaneously presented visual or spatial information that involves visuospatial sketchpad." It explains its own pattern—the Sternberg task's letters activated the phonological loop through subvocal rehearsal, whereas the color-recall and Corsi tasks involved the visuospatial sketchpad. This account organizes the study's task-specific training effects.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable by which WM storage system (visuospatial sketchpad vs phonological loop) they engage
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation offered to explain their null Sternberg result and prior contradictory findings; the article calls for future work on how alpha NF influences neural activity during the color-recall task
target_learners: healthy adults
target_learning_goals: visual working memory capacity and precision
examples: The article contrasts its letter-based modified Sternberg task (phonological loop) with the color-recall and Corsi-block tasks (visuospatial sketchpad) and with Zoefel et al.'s mental-rotation task

article_title: Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning
citation: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5
title: Cross-frequency account: alpha and theta oscillations are temporally coordinated mechanisms for learning versus memory of speech-print mappings
description: The article proposes that alpha oscillations regulate attentional/cognitive resources during the establishment of speech-print associations, while theta oscillations support memory storage and maintenance. It interprets its cross-frequency phase-resetting finding as suggesting "α and θ oscillations as temporally coordinated mechanisms associated with different subprocesses, i.e., the learning (α) and memory (θ), of speech-print mappings." This account aligns the observed alpha-driven 4 and 7 Hz phase resetting in early learning with prior work linking prestimulus alpha to cross-sensory integration and theta to associative memory.
requirements: Future mechanistic tests, for which the authors recommend transcranial magnetic/current stimulation combined with online EEG recording, given the "limited efﬁciency and signal-to-noise ratio of sensory entrainment".
constraints: The phase-resetting evidence was limited to early exposure, congruent trials, and alpha-rate stimulation; theta-rate stimulation showed no behavioral effect in this study.
target_learners: adult learners acquiring novel speech-print associations
children with reading difficulties (proposed application)
target_learning_goals: learning cross-modal associations between speech sounds and written symbols
examples: The authors note the phase-resetting effect was "most evident in the initial stage of learning" and interpret alpha-rate stimulation as possibly suppressing task-irrelevant processing and supporting sustained attention to new information.

article_title: Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training
citation: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z
title: Alternating cued and non-cued practice trials with blocked after-action feedback
description: MT-ITS training alternates cued trials, on which the optimal point of aim is shown, with non-cued trials, and delivers feedback in blocks rather than after every trial. The cued presentations are justified by the Instance Theory of Automatization, which "assumes that practice leads to storing of multiple instances of trained material in memory, thus increasing the speed of retrieval and contributing to effortless performance." Cued and non-cued trials were interleaved to avoid fostering reliance on the cue, and after-action feedback was summarized per trial rather than per shot.
requirements: Requires a system able to compute and display the optimal point of aim and to record per-shot performance for the after-action summary
constraints: The article notes that presenting feedback on only the immediately preceding trial might overwhelm trainees and foster heavy reliance and dependence on this form of feedback
target_learners: novice military shooters training on moving-target engagement
target_learning_goals: automating point-of-aim adjustment for moving targets and reducing dependence on external cues
examples: MT-ITS presented the same target types with and without the aiming cue sequentially, repeating the combination for all target types, and gave after-action feedback as a sequential shot-by-shot presentation plus a statistical summary.

title: ALEKS PPL adaptive placement assessment
description: ALEKS Placement, Preparation and Learning (ALEKS PPL) is an adaptive assessment system based on Knowledge Space Theory that recommends placement in post-secondary mathematics courses. It contains 314 items covering elementary mathematics to precalculus, with a limit of 29 questions. The assessment employs an adaptive querying process where "the student's previous answers affect the choice of the next item to ask." Approximately 97% of assessments reach the maximum limit of 29 questions. Placement recommendations fall into six categories based on item and percentage scores.

Adaptive querying process with probabilistic item classification
constraints: The article notes the purpose of their work is not to validate current course placement recommendations; validity is investigated in other works
Most items have an open-ended free response interface prone to careless errors or slips

target_learning_goals: identifying student knowledge state for course placement
examples: The assessment partitions items into in-state, out-of-state, and uncertain categories, terminating when all items are classified or the maximum of 29 questions is reached

citation: Brender, J., El-Hamamsy, L., Giang, C., Mathex, L., Käser, T., & Mondada, F. (2025). The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10503-z
title: Align new programming tools with teachers' existing classroom practices to increase acceptance

HPL embodies this principle by being paper-based rather than tablet-based, requiring no devices beyond those already in classrooms, and using handwriting, a skill already taught. training transfer to daily work

citation: P. Spangenberger, N. Matthes, F. Kapp, L. Kruse, J. L. Plass. (2025). Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10409-2

description: The article argues that iVR is more effective when its specific affordances (presence, agency, interaction with 3D objects, representing inaccessible or unsafe systems) are matched to the learning objectives rather than used for their own sake. As the authors state, "this medium can be more effective than other media if the learning materials take advantage of the affordances of iVR, that is, where the affordances of iVR are aligned with the learning objectives." design features (e.g., pedagogical agent, miniature models, help view) chosen to support those objectives

troubleshooting comprehension
transfer of technical procedures

citation: Hollands, F., & Escueta, M. (2020). How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 163–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09678-z
title: Australian university's streamlined alpha-launch process for piloting and scaling educational technology
description: A multi-step institutional process for acquiring educational technology, developed by an Academic Director at an Australian university. It combines a prioritized list of technology initiatives informed by external research (Horizon and Gartner reports), a market scan, and a time-boxed pilot: "An alpha launch runs for 6 weeks, or half a semester, with the idea that if it yields positive results, the technology can be in place campus-wide by the beginning of the following semester." The term alpha launch signals no guarantee of continued licensing, countering pilots that inevitably led to long-term use.

Regular stakeholder feedback mechanisms, including a showcase every 6 weeks and a technology list re-prioritized every 6 months

Recommendations about scaling up may be made before some important results (end-of-course grades, longer-term resilience metrics) are available

target_learning_goals: Improving pedagogy and student outcomes through vetted educational technology adoption
examples: An online polling initiative that underwent an alpha launch and was subsequently implemented university-wide

description: The alternating renewal process is a statistical model for the stream of behavior as perceived during an observation session, used to simulate realistic direct-observation data. A recording system (continuous recording, momentary time sampling, partial interval recording, or frequency counting) whose scoring rules can be modeled
constraints: The main-text simulation assumes exponential distributions for episode durations and inter-response times, selected "purely for sake of simplicity"
Prevalence and incidence assumed constant within each phase, though they may change between phases
target_learners: Individual cases in single-case design research (e.g., children with autism, students with challenging behavior)
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement and synthesis of behavioral intervention effects in single-case research
examples: The simulation used the ARPobservation package for R, with a full factorial 4×4×4×3×2×7 design and 2000 simulated phase-pairs per condition

title: Some assessments should allow and encourage AI use to reflect real-world professional practice
description: The guide was reframed from assessing AI resistance to assessing AI vulnerability because AI is now part of professional settings nurses train for. The article states "Some assessments should allow and encourage AI use to facilitate appropriate and effective learning" and that the aim is not to work against AI or LLMs.
requirements: Distinguishing AI as a cognitive extension to support learning from cognitive outsourcing that delegates learning's cognitive tasks to AI
constraints: Unbalanced student AI use may produce faulty mental models, reduced cognitive engagement and retention, and diminished capacity for problem-solving and creativity
target_learners: graduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: appropriate and effective learning with AI aligned to professional practice
examples: The initial guide aimed at assessment resistance to AI; reframing renamed its purpose to AI vulnerability rather than resistance

article_title: The moderating role of self-efficacy in influencing the level of competencies among Middle Nurse Managers: A cross-sectional study.
citation: Ivziku Dhurata, Curcio Felice, Filomeno Lucia, Lachi Alessio, D'Agostino Fabio, Giannetta Noemi, Forte Daniela, Gori Nexhmije, Gonzalez Cesar Ivan Aviles, Tartaglini Daniela. (2026). The moderating role of self‐efficacy in influencing the level of competencies among Middle Nurse Managers: A cross‐sectional study. Journal of Nursing Scholarship. https://doi.org/10.1111/jnu.70121
title: Leadership competency framework integrating cognitive, social, and emotional competencies
description: The study is guided by the leadership competency framework of Almatrooshi et al. (2016), which "integrates transformational and transactional leadership theories and highlights the role of cognitive, social, and emotional competencies in effective leadership and organizational performance". In this study, cognitive competencies were operationalized as educational appropriateness and leadership training intentions; social competencies as autonomy, role clarity, and work complexity; and emotional competencies as leadership self-efficacy. The authors report that their findings extend the framework by showing competence is associated with the interaction of these dimensions.
requirements: Leadership competence is understood through the interaction of individual and organizational factors supporting effective managerial behaviors
constraints: The framework was examined in a cross-sectional design, so causal pathways among the dimensions are not established
target_learners: Middle Nurse Managers in public and private healthcare organizations
target_learning_goals: Leadership competence knowledge
Competence application in managerial practice

citation: Paudel, K. R., Sotto, M., Jack-Edwards, F., & Shetty, P. (2026). Correlation of NBME pharmacology subject exam performance with medical school internal pharmacology scores and academic metrics. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-57653-5
title: Align internal pharmacology curriculum and assessments with the NBME content framework
description: The article recommends aligning the pharmacology curriculum with the NBME content framework so that internal assessments reflect and predict students' pharmacological knowledge. It states these findings "underscore the value of aligning the pharmacology curriculum with the NBME content framework" and suggests regular analysis of internal exam performance relative to NBME outcomes can guide course design improvements.
requirements: Internal assessments developed in alignment with course objectives and consistent item formats across cohorts
constraints: Correlation alone may not establish formal alignment; additional blueprinting or content-mapping studies would be required

target_learning_goals: pharmacology knowledge and application
examples: The study analyzed 290 graduates in a discipline-based curriculum where internal exams used single-response multiple-choice items delivered via ExamSoft

article_title: Effect of case-specific 3D-printed models on surgical performance in cadaveric dissection-a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Omari Adam, Nøhr Anders, Suleiman Elissa, Cayé‑Thomasen Per, Sørensen Mads Sølvsten, Frithioff Andreas, Andersen Steven Arild Wuyts. (2026). Effect of case-specific 3D-printed models on surgical performance in cadaveric dissection—a randomized controlled trial. European Archives of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00405-026-10099-x
title: Align simulator fidelity with learner stage: prefer generic-anatomy models for novices
description: The article concludes that "simulator fidelity should be calibrated to learner stage" in progressive simulation-based curricula, and that "generic-anatomy models should be preferred for novices given better alignment with their foundational learning needs." Functional task alignment matters more than physical resemblance; fine case-specific details may distract novices from basic objectives such as drill control and landmarks.
requirements: Training programs must identify the learner's stage (novice vs. experienced) and the foundational skills the simulation should train
constraints: Case-specific training may still benefit trainees whose anatomy deviates markedly from generic anatomy, e.g., malformations or sclerotic mastoid, and for experienced trainees transitioning to actual patients, though the authors call this speculative
target_learners: novice ORL residents (PGY2-4)
target_learning_goals: mastoidectomy and posterior tympanotomy surgical skills
examples: In the RCT, novices trained on generic-anatomy models transferred better to cadaveric dissection than those trained on case-specific models

article_title: Classroom behavioral indicators predict academic performance in large-class clinical instruction: a cohort study using real-time behavioral data.
citation: Sun Shiying, Xu Shenglin, Wang Xue. (2026). Classroom behavioral indicators predict academic performance in large-class clinical instruction: a cohort study using real-time behavioral data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09340-2
title: Align assessment design with instructional objectives to promote engagement and performance
description: The article argues that evaluative context shapes how students allocate effort and respond to learning tasks. It states these findings "highlight the need for intentional alignment between assessment strategies and instructional goals", particularly in technology-enhanced classrooms where disengagement may not be immediately visible. Examination-based formats were associated with higher answer accuracy than non-examination-based formats in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
requirements: Assessment format must be deliberately chosen to align with instructional objectives rather than left as an incidental course feature
constraints: The association between assessment format and accuracy was observational, with format determined by existing course context rather than random allocation
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in technology-enhanced classrooms
target_learning_goals: promoting engagement and academic performance through assessment design
examples: The study compared examination-based and non-examination-based course formats at the class level as a between-group observational analysis

article_title: Reforming hospital management education with the P-MASE pedagogy: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Zhang Yongshuo, Li Wenbo, Zhang Chuchen, Wang Yawei, Feng Shuo. (2026). Reforming hospital management education with the P-MASE pedagogy: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08948-8
title: Align teaching strategies with competency-based, performance-oriented assessment to narrow the knowing–doing gap
description: From a health professions education perspective, the authors argue findings "support the value of aligning teaching strategies with competency-based, performance-oriented assessment." By integrating problem-based inquiry, authentic task chains, social learning supports, and experiential simulation, P-MASE may help narrow the knowing–doing gap by providing repeated opportunities for learners to apply policy rules, interpret data, and justify decisions under competing constraints within a controlled educational context.
requirements: Performance-based assessment instruments that externalize learners' reasoning processes within standardized tasks
constraints: Educational gains are course-based and short-term; translation to sustained workplace performance would require further workplace-based evaluation with objective, real-world outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate health administration and hospital management students
target_learning_goals: applied reasoning, data interpretation, and decision justification under constraints
examples: The trial aligned each course objective with measurable indicators via a four-dimensional evaluation framework and assessed competencies through standardized simulation and task-based performance

article_title: Integrating formative and summative feedback in online situational judgement tests: effects of feedback design on medical students' motivational and cognitive learning factors.
citation: Reiser, S., Schick, K., Pittroff, S. I. D., Janssen, L., Berberat, P. O., Gartmeier, M., & Bauer, J. (2026). Integrating formative and summative feedback in online situational judgement tests: effects of feedback design on medical students’ motivational and cognitive learning factors. Medical Education Online, 31(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639198
title: Select feedback designs by aligning enrichment strategy and timing with the specific learning outcomes targeted, since no single feedback version optimally fosters all outcomes
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that feedback design be chosen deliberately rather than by general superiority. Because the RCT showed differential effects — expert explanations aiding cognitive and utility outcomes, delayed timing aiding motivational and fairness outcomes — the authors conclude that "an optimal feedback approach depends on specific learning outcomes and student characteristics, highlighting the importance of careful selection of feedback strategies tailored to specific educational goals and contexts." Selecting an appropriate design therefore involves balancing competing objectives such as motivation and cognitive load.
requirements: A multicriteria definition of the targeted learning outcomes (motivational, cognitive-load, perception and benefit variables) before choosing feedback enrichment and timing
constraints: No single feedback version optimally fostered all outcomes simultaneously in this study; medical students' familiarity with test-based assessment may limit generalisability to other groups
target_learners: medical students in higher education
target_learning_goals: medical communication competence
motivation for further learning
self-regulated processing of feedback
examples: The RCT compared four task-based feedback versions (Immediate/Post-Test Reflection, Immediate/Post-Test Explanation) with a Summative Test Profile across four outcome sets
Delayed versions (PR, PE) raised perceived competence, fairness and positive affect, while explanation versions (IE, PE) raised germane load and perceived utility

article_title: Deconstructing Participant Behaviors in Virtual Reality Simulation: Ethnographic Analysis.
citation: Loeb Daniel, Shoemaker Jamie, Ely Kelly, Zackoff Matthew. (2025). Deconstructing Participant Behaviors in Virtual Reality Simulation: Ethnographic Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/65886
title: Align simulation modality with learning objectives: use VR for clinical assessment and cognitive objectives, and complementary modalities for hands-on skill development
description: The article recommends that educators thoughtfully align desired learning objectives with the chosen training modality. Its findings suggest "VR may be better suited for clinical assessment or cognitive objectives over physical skill–based objectives," because navigational challenges and limited physical interaction can break fidelity. The authors state there is "the persistent need for complementary simulation modalities, such as AR and computerized manikin-based simulations, which may better support hands-on skill development."
requirements: Educators must understand how a modality influences participant attention and behavior before assigning learning objectives to it
constraints: Until technical workarounds are unnecessary, experience with hands-on tasks in VR may not support skill acquisition directly applicable to real-life clinical care
target_learners: simulation educators in medical education
clinicians training in pediatric resuscitation
target_learning_goals: clinical assessment and rapid decision-making
physical examination maneuvers and procedural skills
examples: The study's VR scenario focused on recognizing and treating shock, yet participants were at times distracted by needing to relearn how to administer a fluid bolus in VR

article_title: Effect of digital virtual reality simulator on pre-clinical dental surgical skill training: a retrospective study.
citation: Ren Jian-gang, Li Rui-fang, Zhang Wei, Yu Zi-li, Chen Gang. (2025). Effect of digital virtual reality simulator on pre-clinical dental surgical skill training: a retrospective study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07747-x
title: Align preclinical simulation with authentic clinical contexts by integrating theoretical explanation with hands-on virtual practice
description: The article argues preclinical training works best when the simulation environment mirrors real clinical conditions and theory is taught alongside practice. It states that "the format of DVRS provides greater alignment with actual clinical practice, and the detailed explanations in DVRS complement hands-on activities, reinforcing theoretical knowledge concurrently with practical application", which the authors link to "marked improvements in both conceptual understanding and technical proficiency among DVRS trainees". Traditional manikins, by contrast, "do not adequately simulate real-life oral clinical conditions".
requirements: Simulation content that reproduces realistic patient oral conditions and clinical workflow
Integration of explanatory instruction with hands-on operative practice
constraints: Evidence comes from a retrospective two-cohort comparison rather than a randomized trial
target_learners: fourth-year undergraduate stomatology students
target_learning_goals: integration of theoretical knowledge with practical surgical application
preparedness for transition from lab practice to clinical work
examples: DVRS students practiced the whole process of clinical treatment from inquiry to operations on 3D models of real patients and clinical environments

citation: Kim Erin, Tchinde Marius J., Rooney Deborah M., Ngam Blessing N., Rettig R. Luke, Gross Christopher L., Snell Mark J., Barnard Melanie L., El-Hayek Kevin, Jeffcoach David R., Kim Grace J. (2025). A novel tool for assessing psychomotor proficiency in laparoscopic cholecystectomy using simulation-based training. Surgical Endoscopy 39(5):3386–3395. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-11708-2
title: ALL-SAFE cholecystectomy module: an open-source online platform with case-based learning and a user-assembled box trainer costing less than $10 USD
description: ALL-SAFE is "an open-source, online laparoscopic surgery training platform designed for varied-resource settings," developed by surgeons from Africa and the US in partnership with PAACS. The cholecystectomy module pairs an online case-based learning exercise structured with Bloom's taxonomy with a low-cost, self-assembled box trainer and expert video tutorial. "The user-assembled cholecystectomy models (Fig. 1) and ALL-SAFE box trainer (Fig. 2) were designed to be cost-effective, using readily available materials costing less than $10 USD." Users practice in the simulator and upload videos for self, peer, and AI review; the platform hosts five procedural modules to date.
requirements: A video-capable cell phone, laptop computer, and Wi-Fi or Bluetooth connectivity for video submission; blunt grasper, Maryland grasper, scissors, needle driver, and 2–0 silk sutures
constraints: The final module was hosted on a web platform optimized for low-bandwidth settings to enhance accessibility in resource-limited environments
target_learners: Surgeons, residents, and medical students across experience levels in LMIC and HIC hospitals
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and psychomotor skills for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
examples: The study ran from May to July 2024 at eight hospitals, with an LMIC cohort (n = 27) from Cameroon, Kenya, Ethiopia, and Nigeria and an HIC cohort (n = 25) from five US institutions

article_title: Exploring the congruence between perceived parent-teacher achievement goals and student academic outcomes: A study using polynomial regression with response surface analysis.
citation: Zhao, N., Dou, D., Chen, X., Chen, F., Luo, R., Zhu, X., & Xiang, G.-X. (2025). Exploring the congruence between perceived parent–teacher achievement goals and student academic outcomes: A study using polynomial regression with response surface analysis. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 603–626. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12742
title: Align home and school achievement goals, especially mastery goals, to support student achievement
description: The article's central practical implication is that consistency between parents' and teachers' achievement goals supports students' academic performance, so schools should build partnerships that coordinate goals. The authors state that "schools need to establish mutually trusting and respectful home–school partnerships", including communication channels and parent workshops on goal setting. The recommendation rests on the response surface findings that congruence in mastery goals predicted both subjects and congruence in performance goals predicted mathematics.

constraints: Effect sizes were relatively small and the authors caution the overall impact of parent and teacher goals is limited
The performance-goal congruence benefit did not extend to language performance
target_learners: Primary and junior middle school students (Grades 3–8) in China
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Language achievement
examples: The study surveyed 4944 students across five provinces and modelled congruence with polynomial regression and response surface analysis rather than manipulating goal alignment

article_title: Empowering medical students: bridging gaps with high-fidelity simulations; a mixed-methods study on self-efficacy.
citation: Koçkaya Pınar Daylan, Alvur Tuncay Müge, Odabaşı Orhan. (2024). Empowering medical students: bridging gaps with high-fidelity simulations; a mixed-methods study on self-efficacy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05996-w
title: Design ALS training programs that promote and correlate both self-efficacy perception and performance, with regular self-assessment opportunities
description: The authors recommend that ALS training throughout medical education be designed so that self-efficacy perception and performance are both high and correlated, because a disparity between perceived capability and actual performance can endanger patients. They state it is crucial to design programs "that promote high levels of both self-efficacy perception and performance, ensuring they are correlated." Regular opportunities for self-assessment and performance evaluation should be built into curricula with a learner-centered approach.
requirements: Training programs should be carefully designed and integrated into educational curricula with a learner-centered approach
constraints: The article notes that when self-efficacy perception is high but performance inadequate, there are potential risks to the patient
target_learners: final-year medical students in emergency medicine internships
target_learning_goals: advanced life support technical skills
accurate self-assessment of resuscitation competence
examples: The study used video-recorded debriefing and CPR feedback wristbands to give students objective evidence of their compression performance, which students reported as revealing their actual pace and skill level

title: ALS Technical Skills Self-Efficacy Perception (ALS-SEP) Form with 100-mm Visual Analog Scale
description: The ALS-SEP Form is a nine-item self-efficacy perception instrument covering chest compression, airway management, bag valve mask ventilation, endotracheal intubation, vascular access, defibrillation, rhythm recognition, energy setting, and drug administration. It was developed "through consultation with physicians, paramedics, and national ALS trainers" aligned with ERC and AHA guidelines, scored on a 100-mm VAS from 1 ("I certainly cannot do it") to 10 ("I certainly can do it"), administered as pre-test and post-test.
requirements: Administered as a pre-test during the first quarter of the emergency medicine internship and a post-test at the end of the internship
constraints: The article reports low concordance between ALS-SEP scores and observed performance (Kappa < 0.2)
target_learners: medical students in emergency medicine internships
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy perception of ALS technical skills
examples: The form was used to measure percentage change in combined self-efficacy score (CSES) between experimental and control groups

article_title: Do the teaching, practice and assessment of clinical communication skills align?
citation: Dewi Sari Puspa, Amanda Wilson, Robbert Duvivier, Brian Kelly, Conor Gilligan. (2024). Do the teaching, practice and assessment of clinical communication skills align? BMC Medical Education 24:609. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05596-8
title: Align communication skills teaching, practice and assessment across learning environments, with rehearsal and feedback in each setting
description: The article argues that communication curricula should be planned under constructive alignment so that the skills taught, practised and assessed are consistent across classroom, clinical and assessment settings. It recommends that "Students would benefit from opportunities to rehearse and practise in different learning environments and receive feedback on their performance in each setting". Combining formal classroom sessions with experiential clinical learning, observation and feedback is proposed, but its efficacy hinges on alignment including clinician role-modelling.
requirements: Opportunities to rehearse and practise in different learning environments with feedback on performance in each setting
Alignment of teaching, learning and assessment of communication skills across environments, including role-modelling by clinicians
constraints: The article reports the approach's efficacy hinges on alignment and calls for further long-term research; it does not itself test the approach
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills
transfer of skills across learning environments
examples: The studied program ran four interactional skills workshops during the WACH rotation, real patient encounters, and an end-of-rotation multi-station OSCE

article_title: Multi-disciplinary, simulation-based, standardised trauma team training within the Victorian State Trauma System.
citation: Fitzgerald MC, Noonan M, Lim E, Mathew Joseph K, Boo E, Stergiou HE, Kim Y, Reilly S, Groombridge C, Maini A, Williams K, Mitra B. (2022). Multi‐disciplinary, simulation‐based, standardised trauma team training within the Victorian State Trauma System. Emergency Medicine Australasia. https://doi.org/10.1111/1742-6723.14068
title: Alfred Trauma Team Reception and Resuscitation Training (TTRRT) programme
description: A standardised, multi-disciplinary, simulation-based trauma team training programme developed at The Alfred Hospital and delivered across 27 programmes at one major trauma centre, two large suburban hospitals and four regional hospitals. It has three phases (pre-programme survey, attendance and assessment, post-programme evaluation) and comprises prescribed pre-learning, didactic lectures on team dynamics and human factors, four skill stations, low-fidelity simulated team scenarios and structured debriefing. It was "designed to be cost‐effective and easily replicable in resource‐limited settings".
requirements: On-site delivery with local medical or nursing students volunteering as simulated patients
Facilitation by two trauma critical care and/or surgical consultants and two critical care trained emergency nurses
Pre-learning via the Trauma Victoria website and a roles-and-responsibilities manual before face-to-face training
constraints: Only a small proportion of providers within the state trauma system were captured, limiting generalisability; only half of participants completed post-programme feedback
target_learners: Emergency medicine, anaesthesia, intensive care, trauma and surgical medical and nursing staff involved in trauma reception and resuscitation
target_learning_goals: Trauma team leadership and followership
Non-technical skills including communication and decision-making
Life-saving interventions in major trauma reception and resuscitation
examples: 27 programmes delivered over a 2-year period across tertiary, urban and rural settings, with simulation training in situ in resuscitation bays where clinically possible

article_title: Efficiently exploring the causal role of contextual moderators in behavioral science.
citation: Hecht, C. A., Dweck, C. S., Murphy, M. C., Kroeper, K. M., & Yeager, D. S. (2022). Efficiently exploring the causal role of contextual moderators in behavioral science. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 120(1). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2216315120
title: Align growth mindset teaching across both messages and structural opportunities, and avoid substituting warmth or diffuse encouragement for authentic mindset practices
description: A practice recommendation drawn from the article's causal evidence: teachers should communicate growth mindset support "not only in what they say but also in their class policies", because study 3 showed the mindset–choice link was strongest only when messages and opportunities were aligned. Teachers should also "avoid using “false” growth mindset practices" such as being nice or giving diffuse encouragement, since study 4 showed a warm demeanor did not offset fixed mindset messaging.
requirements: Teachers must actually afford structural opportunities such as grading policies that reward improvement, not merely endorse growth mindset beliefs verbally
constraints: Evidence comes from scenarios depicting a hypothetical math teacher and a short-term choice outcome, so the article positions these as guidance for future teacher-level field experiments rather than tested classroom intervention effects
target_learners: Adolescent students in secondary mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' enactment of growth mindset beliefs through learning-oriented choices such as selecting challenging tasks
examples: Study 3 crossed fixed versus growth messages with fixed versus growth opportunities; study 4 contrasted firm and warm fixed mindset teachers to rule out warmth as an active ingredient

title: WADA's ALPHA e-learning anti-doping programme (Zh-hans version)
description: ALPHA (Athlete Learning Program about Health and Anti-Doping) is WADA's interactive e-learning seminar, translated into Chinese by CHINADA in 2020. It consists of 8 modules covering the doping control process, whereabouts, therapeutic use exemptions, results management, medical and ethical reasons not to dope, practical help to stay clean, and dealing with pressure. Modules 7–8 use "an 'if–then' plan, scenario-based learning, and video testimonials from elite athletes". In this study it was delivered on a computer screen in a fixed module sequence taking approximately 80 min.
requirements: Learners complete all 8 modules in the same sequence; the seminar was monitored with screen recording software to ensure completion
constraints: The article notes the newer 2021 WADA platform removed modules 7–8 offering practical help, restricting the practical value of the findings regarding attitudes and likelihood
target_learners: Chinese college athletes
non-athlete young adults
target_learning_goals: anti-doping knowledge
negative attitudes towards doping
practical strategies to resist pressure to dope
examples: In this study the ALPHA seminar was presented on a 24'' computer screen at a viewing distance of approximately 80 cm, with all participants completing each module in the same sequence

article_title: Can I Have Your Recipe? Using a Fidelity of Implementation (FOI) Framework to Identify the Key Ingredients of Formative Assessment for Learning.
citation: Offerdahl E. G., McConnell M., Boyer J. (2018). Can I Have Your Recipe? Using a Fidelity of Implementation (FOI) Framework to Identify the Key Ingredients of Formative Assessment for Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-02-0029
title: Align formative assessment prompts with stated learning outcomes so the evidence produced permits diagnosis of gaps
description: The article argues that effective formative assessment prompts must align with stated learning outcomes, because "it is impossible to diagnose student progress, let alone revise instruction or generate meaningful feedback" without a clear indication of the desired outcome. Prompts must uncover students' current understanding relative to the desired level of understanding. The article illustrates how a muddiest-point paper misaligned with an argumentation outcome is a potentially unproductive adaptation, whereas a minute paper asking students to generate and justify a claim from a graph is potentially productive.
requirements: Clear learning outcomes stating what students need to know or be able to do, against which prompt evidence can be diagnosed
constraints: Misaligned outcomes and prompts are not likely to produce information that allows instructors or students to diagnose gaps between present and desired levels of understanding
target_learners: Undergraduate life sciences students
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis of progress toward stated learning outcomes
examples: Adapting a minute paper to ask students to generate and justify one claim from a graph, to reveal skills of data interpretation and claim generation essential to scientific argumentation

article_title: Student engagement, assessed using heart rate, shows no reset following active learning sessions in lectures.
citation: Darnell, D. K., & Krieg, P. A. (2019). Student engagement, assessed using heart rate, shows no reset following active learning sessions in lectures. PLoS ONE 14(12): e0225709. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0225709
title: Value active learning for the activity itself, not for an expected attention reset afterward
description: The article concludes that because HR shows no reset after active learning, "the value of AL is restricted to the activities contained within that episode and not to an upward reset of student engagement after the active period." Course designers should therefore justify AL time by the learning done within the activity, not by expected gains in attention during following didactics.
requirements: Active learning sessions such as think-pair-share or paired problem solving inserted into lectures
constraints: Findings based on HR as a surrogate measure in medical school lectures; no reset was observed for activities averaging about 5 minutes in length
target_learners: first-year medical students
target_learning_goals: maintaining engagement during lectures
designing active learning sessions within didactic lectures
examples: The study analyzed 22 AL events, ten think-pair-share discussions and twelve problem-solving sessions with neighbor discussion, in medical school lectures
